Nearly every survey is unrepresentative, and nearly every question is about a population. These ten entries cover how to get from one to the other, how to tell when the adjustment hasn't worked, and how to show the results.

## Part 1: From a sample to a population

1. **[Mister P](../concepts/mister-p.qmd).** Multilevel regression and poststratification: estimates for states and subgroups from a sample with the wrong mix.
2. **[Theoretical and Applied Statisticians, how to tell them apart](../concepts/theoretical-vs-applied-statisticians.qmd).** Model the outcome given the covariates, then average over the population you care about.
3. **[The Groovy Grandma Problem](../concepts/groovy-grandma-problem.qmd).** Weighting fixes the variables you weight on, and nothing else.
4. **[Canary variable](../concepts/canary-variable.qmd).** Hold back a variable whose population value you know, and use it to check the adjustment.
5. **[What would you do if you had all the data?](../concepts/if-you-had-all-the-data.qmd).** Decide what you are estimating before deciding how.

## Part 2: Seeing and reporting the results

6. **[The Secret Weapon](../concepts/secret-weapon.qmd).** Fit the same model to every survey year and plot all the estimates together.
7. **[The Superplot](../concepts/superplot.qmd).** Rich people vote Republican and rich states vote Democratic, in one graph.
8. **[The USA Today Fallacy](../concepts/usa-today-fallacy.qmd).** An average over states is not an average over people.
9. **[Second-Order Availability Bias](../concepts/second-order-availability-bias.qmd).** The correlations in your own circle are not the population's.
10. **[The Australia principle](../concepts/australia-principle.qmd).** When the data can't measure a tiny difference, the prior has to.
